turns.answer:
Our Senior Pastor teaches that good works are not the price we pay to be saved, but rather they are the result and proof of our salvation.

She explains that good works serve as evidence that we are saved, a sign that we have received the divine nature of God [1]. Just as God Himself does good works, such as creating the heavens and the earth and declaring it "very good," when we do good works, we are proving that we are like our Father [1]. Forgiving others or being generous are examples of good works that demonstrate the changed nature we have received, as God's nature is generous (John 3:16) [1]. She emphasizes that the believer is not saved as a result of good works, but good works are the result of salvation [1][3]. It is only under the law that people worked for salvation; as new creations, we do good works because we are justified and it is our nature, not to earn God's approval, as He has already approved us [3].

Our Senior Pastor also teaches that good works are part of God's plan, predating our birth, both biological and spiritual [4]. God pre-ordained us unto good works just as He pre-ordained us unto salvation, with His will being for every new creation to do the good works that are in Christ Jesus (Ephesians 2:10) [4][9][16]. These works are not naturally done by people; good works are the result of God working in the believer's heart [3].

Specifically, the "good works" God has ordained for us are primarily the works of ministry, not things like building roads or houses [2]. We are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God had before ordained that we should walk in them (Ephesians 2:10) [2][9][16]. This includes joining Jesus in His work, going about doing good, and healing all oppressed by the devil, because God is with us [14]. Salvation gives purpose and meaning to our lives, directing us to these good works [14].

Salvation itself is entirely a gift from God, received by grace through faith, not by works, so no one can boast (Ephesians 2:8-9) [2][9][16]. It is a complete package, accomplished through Christ's death, burial, and resurrection for the salvation and deliverance of men from sin [5]. Our Senior Pastor highlights that everything pertaining to life and godliness was completed in the work of redemption; there is nothing else God needs to do that He has not already done [5]. We are saved by God's mercy, which is the basis of all Jesus did in redemption, saving us from sin, death, and condemnation [7]. We are made righteous by what Jesus did, specifically by His resurrection (2 Corinthians 5:21) [8]. This righteousness allows us to stand before God as if we never sinned, meaning we are justified by His grace [7].

The Holy Spirit's power is essential for these good works of ministry. Our Senior Pastor teaches that the primary purpose of the Holy Spirit's power in a believer's life is for the work of ministry (Acts 1:8) [11]. This power is not for show-off, but for good works of ministry, for edification, not destruction [2][18]. When we preach the gospel or disciple others, we are using the power of God correctly [18]. This power makes us witnesses of the finished work of Christ and the work of redemption [11].

It is crucial to understand that salvation cannot be earned through works, nor is there a second chance after death to work for salvation [17]. God's longsuffering and goodness offer an opportunity for repentance in this life [17].

What is the role of the Holy Spirit?
How does God's plan include good works?

turns.answer:
Our Senior Pastor teaches that discipleship is the structured followership of Jesus Christ that transforms believers to walk in the fullness of God's plan and the realities of eternal life.

Discipleship is not just about learning to know, but about learning to do and to experience the truths of God's word [1]. When we come to church, we must come to be discipled, allowing change and transformation to take place in our lives as we conform to the image of Christ [1]. Our Senior Pastor emphasizes that salvation is just the glorious beginning; discipleship allows us to become everything more that God has ordained for us in Christ [3]. Jesus Himself dedicated 40 days to prepare for His ministry of preaching the gospel and making disciples, highlighting the seriousness of this assignment (Matthew 4:1-17) [7]. The ultimate call for us is to preach the gospel to people, get them saved, and then get them discipled [7].

The local church is described as the wisdom of God and the ordained place for discipleship to happen, much like a home provides nourishment and growth for a child (Matthew 28:19-20) [3]. After salvation, being brought into the light means being in a spiritual home where one can grow, develop, and be nurtured [3]. Discipleship is crucial because, without it, a converted person might continue to act according to their old nature; it is essential to teach them how to live this new life in Christ [13]. It helps us unlearn the old ways and deal with the habits formed before salvation (Ephesians 2:1-3) [8][16].

Our Senior Pastor explains that discipleship is "the missing link" for a believer who has received Christ's life but still struggles with old ways of living [11]. The power to say no to sin and have dominion over it has already been given to us (Romans 6:14), and discipleship helps manifest this power in changing our minds, speech, actions, and life direction [11][14]. It imparts disciplines that lead to growth and usefulness, akin to the regimented life of a soldier (2 Timothy 2:1-5) [15]. This structured approach helps believers overcome the flesh's resistance to spiritual things like prayer and Bible reading, which can otherwise lead to a carnal life [5]. A walk with God, sustained by discipleship, is a walk of power, prosperity, and greatness, bringing about a total transformation, as seen in the life of Abraham (Genesis 17:1-2) [4][6].

A disciple is a student, and Christianity is scholarly, involving teaching, learning, and training [12]. Humility and teachability are very key for a disciple, who must faithfully pass down exactly what they have been taught, communicating the truth of God's Word rather than personal opinions (2 Timothy 2:1-2) [17]. This process transforms individuals like Peter, who, through discipleship, became a powerful soul winner after previously denying Christ [2]. Ultimately, if more believers are discipled, the world will become a better place because discipleship teaches how to navigate every aspect of life, from being an employer to an employee and living with others [10]. Through discipleship, mistakes and errors no longer count, and old things pass away, making everything new [6].

How does discipleship transform a believer?

Our Senior Pastor teaches that boldness is essential for a believer's life, including for fulfilling God's plans and ministry, and it stems from confidence in God and fellowship with Him [3][12][13].

She explains that boldness can be understood through several key points:
1.  **Boldness can be seen** Our Senior Pastor notes that boldness is visible, not primarily through facial expressions, but through the words spoken. The unfettered outspokenness of Peter and John, for instance, demonstrated their boldness [17][18]. It is primarily expressed through speaking freely and without hindrance [13][18]. However, boldness is also expressed through the actions one takes, the choices one makes, and the direction one follows in life [18].
2.  **Supernatural boldness does not come from any natural source** This type of boldness is a gift from God, received through His Holy Spirit. Peter and John's boldness was observed because "they had been with Jesus" (Acts 4:13), indicating that their supernatural boldness was traceable to their fellowship with Him [4][7][17][18].
3.  **Boldness implies unwavering confidence and unshakeable assurance** It is an indication of what or whom you rely on [18]. Your boldness in life is an evidence and testament of where your confidence lies [12]. As believers, our confidence should be placed in God alone because He is our Father, and we are marked by the blood of the everlasting covenant [12]. Trusting in God empowers our boldness in life [12].
4.  **Fellowship with God is crucial for boldness** If you find it difficult to speak about Jesus, checking the state of your fellowship with God is important [4]. Your ministration should be an outflow of your personal fellowship with God, as you cannot effectively witness to something or someone you do not know [9]. Consistent fellowship with the Lord, through a vibrant prayer life and engaging with His Word, strengthens you, refreshes you, and makes you bold to speak about Jesus [2][4][9]. Every time you behold God's face, His boldness rubs off on you, and increasing in knowledge of God makes you bolder to speak about Him [9].
5.  **Cultivating a walk with God** Our Senior Pastor emphasizes establishing a personal devotion routine, often called quiet time, where you read your Bible and pray daily [1]. This practice is vital for spiritual growth, understanding God's Word and ways, and allowing His truth to direct your life [1]. Being prayerless is dangerous for a preacher of the Word because the message is powerful and a threat to the kingdom of darkness, requiring fortification and spiritual soundness [2].

Our Senior Pastor also highlights that God is pleased when we use the faith He has given us, which results in us acting and living like Him and experiencing His results [8][10]. Boldness is the antidote to fear, which can incapacitate and limit a person [5]. She encourages believers to be bold and confident, knowing that anything done on a supernatural level will yield supernatural manifestations and results [14][16].

turns.answer:
Our Senior Pastor teaches that salvation is a gift from God, received by grace through faith, and that good works are the result and proof of this salvation, rather than the means by which it is obtained.

She emphasizes that we are saved by God's mercy and grace, not by any good deeds or attempts to keep the law (Ephesians 2:8-9) [2][7][9][16]. Salvation is a gift, freely given, and we don't pay for it; therefore, there is no room for boasting in our own efforts [9]. The complete work of redemption, which secures our salvation, was accomplished by Jesus Christ on the cross, providing everything that pertains to life and godliness [5][7]. Understanding this work of redemption through faith in Christ Jesus is the foundational knowledge for many aspects of our lives, including family and marriage [15]. Our Senior Pastor reminds us that we are to be grateful for salvation above all else, as it is the "door or key" that opens the door to every other blessing we enjoy in Christ [6]. She also makes it clear that there is no second chance for salvation after death; the choice to accept God's gift must be made "here and now" [17].

Conversely, good works are the natural outcome and evidence of a transformed life. They are the proof of our salvation and a sign that we have received God's divine nature [1][3]. Just as God Himself does good works, when believers extend forgiveness or demonstrate generosity, they are proving that their nature has been changed to be like their Father (John 3:16) [1]. We do good works not to earn God's approval, but because we are already justified and approved by Him, and it is now our nature [3].

These good works are not an afterthought but are deeply embedded in God's eternal plan. Our Senior Pastor teaches that we are God's workmanship, "created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God has before ordained that we should walk in them" (Ephesians 2:10) [2][9][16]. This plan for our good works predates our birth, both biological and spiritual, meaning God had specific assignments prepared for us even before we were born again [4][9][14][16]. God's will is that every new creation should engage in these good works [4].

When speaking of "good works," our Senior Pastor primarily refers to the "good works of ministry," rather than merely building roads or houses [2]. We are created to join Jesus in His work of "doing good and healing all that were oppressed of the devil" (Acts 10:38) [9][14]. The power of God, received through the Holy Spirit, is essential for these good works of ministry. This power is given to believers to be witnesses (Acts 1:8) and is intended for the salvation of men and for edification, not for destruction (2 Corinthians 13:10) [11][18]. It enables us to preach the gospel, pray for the sick, and disciple others, and God also provides ministry gifts to equip us for this calling [13][18].
